summary: Outlines several models for policy based routing and reviews the relative benefits of each approach. It encourages discussion to move toward the model that scales best in a large internetwork.

eli5.summary: There are many ways to make rules for traffic paths. This compares them side by side and asks people which one would work best for a huge network.

questions: which policy routing model scales best
what are the models of policy based routing
subtitle: Three ways to enforce network usage rules, compared on goals, benefits, concerns and costs.

tldr.problem: Network operators want to control who may use scarce network resources, but there are several different ways to do it and each has different strengths and costs.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes three models, policy based distribution of routing information, policy based packet filtering and forwarding, and policy based dynamic allocation of network resources, and reviews each one's goals, benefits, concerns and costs. It also separates policy routing from accounting.
tldr.outcome: It is a discussion paper that invites comments toward the model that scales best in a large internetwork, and it does not define a protocol.

sections.title: Three Models of Policy Routing
sections.content:
The memo says three models are most often referenced: policy based distribution of routing information, policy based packet filtering/forwarding, and policy based dynamic allocation of network resources such as bandwidth and buffers. Each was designed for a particular set of requirements, and sometimes more than one must be implemented.

They work at different granularity. The first is formulated at the Administrative Domain or network number level, the second down to end systems or even individual users, and the third at end systems, local routers, Routing Domains and Administrative Domains. They can be combined, and the resource model is described as orthogonal to the routing information model, though they may interact in practice.

The memo argues that policy based routing gives a predictable, stable result based on the administrator's wishes, whereas uncontrolled dynamic routing may behave better in real time but is less predictable. In a production network, consistent and acceptable service is imperative.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to make traffic rules: control the maps, check every package, or control how much road each group gets. You can also mix them.

sections.title: Model 1: Distributing Routing Information by Policy
sections.content:
The goal is to enforce flows by controlling which routes are announced, at the network or Administrative Domain (AD) level. The memo calls these macroscopic policies. The example is the NSFNET and its interfaces to mid-level networks, where incoming routing information is checked by four means: peer authentication by source address, verification of the AD identification (then EGP Autonomous System numbers), verification of the advertised network numbers, and control of metrics through a Routing Policy Data Base. Outbound announcements are controlled by the same database. The memo states this implementation has been in place since July 1988.

Benefits: it allows engineering of large wide area networks in a more meshed environment, and has almost no performance cost because only the routing packets are subject to policy. Concerns: it does not address packet filtering, for instance it cannot stop malicious source routed IP packets, and it does not reach end systems or users. Costs: the routing database needs ongoing upkeep and knowledge of the Internet, covering the more than 1300 networks then in the Internet, though the work can be distributed.
sections.eli5: This is like deciding which roads show up on a map you hand out. It is cheap and fast, but it cannot stop one particular car that is already on the road.

sections.title: Model 2: Filtering and Forwarding Packets by Policy
sections.content:
Here policy is enforced per packet, at the end system or even individual user level, which the memo calls microscopic policies. An implemented example is a protection feature in the NSFNET nodes that filters by IP destination so that the nodes can protect themselves against packets aimed at the NSFNET. It was fully implemented but not enabled, and could be turned on within seconds. A broader scheme is outlined in RFC 1102.

The main benefit is tight control down to individual end systems and perhaps users, and policies carried in packets could even let users move between locations. The main concern is router performance, because each packet would be checked against a policy database, which the memo calls questionable with then-current Internet technology though possibly suitable for circuit switched or connection-oriented networks. Scaling may need hierarchy, which may conflict with arbitrary Type of Service routing.

For cost, the memo estimates 1300 networks with an average of 200 end systems each, giving over 260000 end systems, and notes that the policy database could become immense.
sections.eli5: This is a guard checking every single package at the gate. It is very precise, but if there are a huge number of packages the guard gets overwhelmed.

sections.title: Model 3: Allocating Resources by Policy
sections.content:
The goal is flexible, economical allocation of resources such as bandwidth and buffers according to current needs, with policies set at the network or AD level and possibly by traffic type, for example Telnet, FTP, precedence indicators and network control traffic. Enforcement could be in routers, circuit switches or end systems.

The memo gives two forms. At the circuit level, bandwidth is reconfigured, as in the IDNX component of the NSFNET and the MCI Digital Reconfiguration Service (DRS) planned for the NSFNET. At the packet level, multiple queues give precedence to critical traffic, as in NSFNET nodes preferring traffic tied to the NSFNET backbone network number so that routing information and monitoring get through.

Benefits include bandwidth created as needed, possible cost savings, and no impact on routing protocols or forwarding performance. Concerns are that policies for dynamic allocation in a packet switching environment are still in development, that one AD's tuning could make traffic pass poorly in another AD's network, and that sharing policy across multiple ADs raises political problems needing more study.
sections.eli5: Instead of blocking anyone, this model changes how much road each kind of traffic gets, such as wider lanes for emergency vehicles. But widening your lane might squeeze a neighbor, so you have to talk to them.

sections.title: Discussion and Accounting
sections.content:
The first two models both aim to enforce flows and control access to scarce resources, differing mainly in macroscopic versus microscopic enforcement. If enforcement costs more than making the resource less scarce, its feasibility is questionable. Local policies should not affect global Internet traffic, and transit domains such as the NSFNET should not be affected by one network's local policy. The memo also questions a complex scenario of selling spare link capacity, suggesting that dropping underused links, as the NSFNET planned with the DRS, may be cleaner.

Accounting is related but separate. It combines history with policy information to track usage, and can be done at AD, network, host or user level, and can drive policy. It has the same scaling concerns, plus the burden of gathering and reliably retrieving large amounts of data. The memo suggests a lightweight option of monitoring traffic patterns and reacting to abuse by changing routing policy or blocking hosts or nets, with the caveat that a statistical approach may be slow to react.
sections.eli5: Counting who used how much is a different job from setting the rules, though the two can help each other. Counting everything in great detail is expensive, so a light check for troublemakers may be enough.
